name_en: Anji Bai Cha (Anji White Tea, a green tea)
cultivar: Baiye Yihao (White Leaf No. 1), a temperature-sensitive albino cultivar
processing: Baked green: the pale shoots are withered briefly, pan-fired or hot-air killed, gently straightened into their 'phoenix feather' shape, and dried with warm air; no rolling to speak of and no withering in the white-tea sense.
harvest_season: A short spring window of about a month, usually from late March or early April into late April and sometimes later in a cool year, while the new leaves are still pale; once the weather warms and the leaves turn green the tea loses what makes it special.
appearance_dry: Slender, slightly flattened straight shoots in pale jade and ivory, with the leaf veins faintly visible.
appearance_liquor: Very pale, almost clear with a hint of green-gold.
appearance_wet: Translucent white-jade leaves with green veins, bud and one or two leaves, startlingly pale.
taste_profile: Intensely savoury and sweet, like a light chicken broth with fresh bamboo shoot and a hint of lily, soft and almost without bitterness.

brewing.notes: Glass, 75–80 °C, and go easy on the leaf. The high amino-acid content means it is sweet and savoury at low temperatures and merely grassy at high ones.

vintage_note: Sold only as the current year's spring harvest, and only from a window of a few weeks; pre-Qingming lots are the palest and most expensive, mid-April lots are greener and cheaper. The same cultivar is now planted across Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Guizhou and elsewhere and sold as 'bai cha', so the Anji origin is a protected label worth asking about. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Anji Bai Cha is the tea that confuses everyone on name alone: it is called 'white tea' but it is a green tea. The 'white' is the leaf itself. The Baiye Yihao cultivar it is made from is a natural albino: in the cool weeks of early spring its new shoots come out pale ivory with green veins, and only as the weather warms do they turn ordinary green. The pale leaves are very low in chlorophyll and unusually high in amino acids, which is where the tea's savoury sweetness comes from.

The mother bush was found in the hills of Anji county, in northern Zhejiang, in the 1970s or early 1980s depending on the account, and propagated from cuttings; everything sold under the name descends from it. The leaf is handled gently, fired, lightly straightened into a slim feather shape and dried with warm air, with none of the pressing of Longjing, so it keeps its pale colour and its delicacy.

In the cup it is unlike any other green: a clear, almost colourless liquor that tastes like a light broth, sweet, savoury, with fresh bamboo shoot and a faint lily note, and practically no bitterness. It is best in a glass so you can see the white leaves with green veins open up. Keep the water around 75–80 °C and use a little less leaf than usual; it does not reward strength, and hot water just makes it grassy.

The harvest window is short, a few weeks from late March, because once the leaves green up the tea becomes an ordinary green. That scarcity, plus the fact that the cultivar is now grown far outside Anji, means the label matters: 'Anji' is a protected origin, while 'bai cha' or 'baiye yihao' from Guizhou or Jiangsu can be decent but is cheaper and usually less fine. Look for very pale, even shoots; greenish leaf means late picking.

If you like this umami style, Japanese gyokuro is the obvious comparison; among Chinese teas, a good pre-Qingming Longjing is the nearest cousin.
history:
Anji Bai Cha is a young tea with an old-sounding name. Accounts of its start differ slightly: Chinese sources describe local agricultural workers finding a single wild pale-leaved bush at Guijiachang in Daxi village, Tianhuangping, in the 1970s, while others give 1982 as the year the cultivar was discovered. Everyone agrees on the next step. In the 1980s technicians working on a tea-breeding base in Huzhou, Liu Yimin among them, multiplied the plant from cuttings and brought it down from the mountain into wide planting.

The brand as such dates only from about 1990. Before that the county had a tea called Anji Baipian, and the wild-tree discovery gave the new product its name. Local writing likes to link it to the 'white tea' praised in Emperor Huizong's Song dynasty tea treatise, but nothing ties that tea to this bush.

Its rise was quick. The pale leaf is a temporary low-temperature albinism, and the high amino acid content made a good selling point; a Chinese pun on 'Anji' and the word for amino acid helped. It became a Chinese protected geographical indication on 6 April 2004 and appeared in the 2020 China-EU geographical indications agreement. Planting has since spread to neighbouring Changxing and well beyond Zhejiang.
